newsitem.title: USA: Maine court rejects Green Party's ballot claim.
newsitem.headline: Maine court rejects Green Party's ballot claim.

text.p: The Maine Supreme Court Friday rejected the Green Party's claim it was improperly disqualified from the state ballot because of the poor showing of its 1996 presidential candidate.

The justices ruled unanimously that state law required parties holding ballot status to get at least 5 percent support for both presidential and gubernatorial candidates. Maine votes for one of those offices every two years.

The Green Party qualified for the Maine ballot when its 1994 gubernatorial candidate, Jonathan Carter, got 7 percent of the vote. Its 1996 presidential hopeful, consumer activist Ralph Nader, received less than 2 percent support.

The Maine Greens maintain that it is unfair to require their presidential candidate to meet the 5 percent threshold because the state-based party does not have the organisation needed to field viable candidates for national office.

Friday's ruling sends the case back to U.S. District Court, where a judge is considering if Maine's law is unconstitutional. A Green official acknowledged privately the ruling was a blow to their federal lawsuit.

Maine Secretary of State Dan Gwadowsky expressed satisfaction with the ruling but said he might ask the legislature to change the law to address the Green Party's concerns. Lawmakers have twice rejected similar requests.

The Republican, Democrat and Reform parties currently have ballot status in Maine. Before the Green Party was designated a "major political party" with 1994 election results, its candidates ran as independents.
